ECE 6612

TCP sequence and acknowledgement numbers

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a browser request and a server reply, with each sequence number belonging to its sender and each acknowledgement referring to the other sender.

TCP presents applications with a reliable, ordered byte stream in each direction. A connection is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port, often called its four-tuple. Each endpoint numbers the bytes it sends. The browser and server therefore keep two separate sequence spaces, even though their traffic shares a connection.

SEQ in a segment identifies the first payload byte carried by that sender. ACK identifies the next sequence number that sender expects from its peer. An ACK of 4080 cumulatively acknowledges all preceding bytes through 4079, assuming a continuous received stream. ACK numbers travel in the reverse direction from the bytes they acknowledge.

For an accepted in-order segment starting at sequence s with L payload bytes, the next expected number is s + L. More generally its sequence-space length is L + S + F, where S is 1 when SYN is set and F is 1 when FIN is set, otherwise each is 0. SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. A pure ACK has L = S = F = 0 and consumes none. IP, TCP and link headers do not count as TCP payload bytes.

During connection setup, the client chooses an initial sequence number x and the server independently chooses y. The initial SYN has SEQ x. The SYN-ACK has SEQ y and ACK x+1. The final empty ACK has SEQ x+1 and ACK y+1. Thus x and y come from the endpoints, rather than from packet sizes or from one another. Implementations choose initial values to make blind prediction harder.

Once data flows, advance only the sequence space that carried those bytes. In Fig. 1 the browser sends 80 bytes, advancing the server’s ACK by 80. The server’s own SEQ starts at 9000 because the browser was already expecting that server byte. The server’s 24-byte reply advances its next SEQ to 9024 after sending. It does not change the ACK of browser bytes unless more browser data arrives.

A lost section of the stream stops cumulative ACK progress. If bytes 1000–1099 and 1200–1299 arrive while 1100–1199 are missing, the receiver still ACKs 1100. Selective acknowledgement can additionally report later received ranges. Fig. 2 uses in-order delivery without retransmissions or sequence-number wraparound; actual TCP sequence arithmetic is modulo 2^32.

Example

An established client sends SEQ 7200, ACK 15000 and 60 payload bytes. With no other traffic, the server replies with SEQ 15000 and ACK 7260. If its reply carries 40 bytes, its next fresh data SEQ is 15040; the client’s next data SEQ remains 7260.

Sources and scope
  • Course sequence: Transport Layer Security; original byte-ledger examples complement packet-capture reasoning.
  • RFC 9293, sequence numbers, acknowledgement and connection establishment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html

Practice

1. A client sends SEQ 12000, ACK 45000 and 90 payload bytes. The server immediately replies with 30 payload bytes. Give the server’s SEQ and ACK and the client’s ACK after receiving the reply. Assume in-order delivery with no SYN, FIN or other traffic.

Place client bytes and server bytes on separate number lines.

The server uses SEQ 45000 and ACK 12090. Its reply covers server bytes 45000–45029, so the client then ACKs 45030. The 90 client bytes affect the acknowledgement of client data; the 30 server bytes affect the acknowledgement of server data.

2. Client SYN has SEQ 700 and server SYN-ACK has SEQ 9800. Give the final empty ACK’s SEQ and ACK, then the server’s ACK after the client sends its first 12 data bytes.

Each SYN consumes one sequence number before the data starts.

The final ACK uses SEQ 701 and ACK 9801. The client’s first data bytes are 701–712, so the server acknowledges 713. The empty final ACK itself consumed no sequence number.
